evals.prompt: We're deciding between google/wire and uber-go/dig for a new Go service's dependency injection. What's the actual difference, and how does it affect when we find out about a missing dependency?
evals.expected_output: Explains wire generates real Go code at build time (wire_gen.go) via wire.Build, so a missing/ambiguous provider fails at build/codegen time, while dig resolves dependencies at runtime via reflection, so a missing provider only fails the first time that type is actually resolved/invoked.

assertions.text: Identifies dig as runtime/reflection based, with errors surfacing at Invoke time

evals.prompt: Using uber-go/fx, write the fx.Invoke function that registers an OnStart/OnStop lifecycle hook for an *http.Server so it starts listening when the fx app starts and shuts down gracefully when it stops.
evals.expected_output: Uses fx.Lifecycle's Append method with an fx.Hook containing OnStart and OnStop functions that take a context.Context and return an error, calling the server's start/shutdown methods inside them.

assertions.text: Uses fx.Lifecycle / lc.Append with an fx.Hook
Defines both OnStart and OnStop callbacks

evals.prompt: What's the practical difference between samber/do and uber-go/dig, given they're both runtime dependency injection containers for Go?
evals.expected_output: Explains samber/do uses Go generics (Provide[T], Invoke[T]/MustInvoke[T]) so calls are type-checked at compile time on the calling side, while dig resolves constructor arguments via reflection over interface{} without that compile-time type safety on the call site, even though both still resolve the dependency graph at runtime.

assertions.text: Identifies reflection as dig's mechanism, contrasted with do
